clip.title: TMS
clip.dialogue:
How global giants like Amazon, DHL or {{blank}} manage thousands of shipments every single day without losing control?
The answer lies in one powerful system, the transportation management system or TMS.
In today's video, we'll break down what TMS really is, how it works, and why it's becoming a must-have tool for every modern supply chain.
{{blank}} start.
One, what is a {{blank}} management system, TMS?
A transportation management system, TMS, is a software platform designed to manage, automate, and optimize transportation operations.
It serves as a central hub that connects shippers, carriers, freight forwarders, and customers to ensure goods are moved {{blank}} and cost-effectively.
In simple {{blank}}, a TMS answers three critical questions.
How should we {{blank}} our goods? Planning.
Who should move them? Execution.
How well did we perform? Optimization and reporting.
Two, core functions of a TMS.
A TMS performs several integrated functions across the transportation life cycle.
A. Planning and optimization. Determines the best transportation mode, road, air, sea, rail based on cost, time, and service level.
Suggests {{blank}} routes and load consolidation to minimize cost per shipment.
Uses algorithms to balance cost, delivery {{blank}}, and resource utilization.
Example, a TMS might recommend combining two half truck shipments from nearby suppliers into a single full truckload to save 30% on freight cost.
B. Execution. {{blank}} carrier selection, shipment booking and dispatching.
Generates documentation like bills of lading, shipment manifests, customs paperwork, etc.
Provides real-{{blank}} tracking of vehicles and shipments through GPS and IoT devices.
Example, once an order is ready, TMS automatically assigns the shipment to the most cost-{{blank}} carrier based on contracted rates and availability.
C. Freight settlement and payment. Automates the freight audit process, {{blank}} carrier invoices with contracted rates to detect over billing.
Processes {{blank}} to carriers and integrates with accounting systems.
Helps {{blank}} total landed cost per shipment.
Example, if a {{blank}} bills $2,500, but the contracted rate is $2,300, the TMS flags the discrepancy before payment is released.
D. Reporting and analytics. Generates reports on carrier performance, cost analysis, {{blank}} efficiency, and on-time delivery.
Enables data-driven decision-making by analyzing freight spend, {{blank}} footprint, and shipment patterns.
Example, a TMS dashboard might show that air freight costs rose 12% last {{blank}}, prompting management to explore multimodal transport.
Three, how does a TMS work? Step-by-step process.
Let's {{blank}} down how a transportation management system operates in a typical supply chain environment.
{{blank}} one, data integration. The TMS connects with other enterprise systems such as ERP, enterprise resource planning for order and inventory data, WMS, warehouse management system for shipment readiness and loading, carrier systems for rate contracts and capacity availability.
This creates a unified data ecosystem where all shipment {{blank}} information flows seamlessly.
Step two, planning and {{blank}}.
Once customer orders are received, the TMS consolidates shipments, chooses the best mode, e.g. truckload versus LTL, plans routes based on distance, delivery deadlines and {{blank}}, assigns carriers based on cost and performance.
Modern TMS systems use AI and machine learning to continuously refine planning accuracy and optimize route selection.
Step three, execution. After {{blank}}, the system generates shipping orders and labels.
Communicates with carriers via EDI, {{blank}} data interchange or APIs.
Tracks shipments using GPS, RFID or IoT enabled sensors.
Sends real-time updates to customers on shipment status.
Step four, freight {{blank}}. Once shipments are delivered, the TMS validates carrier invoices against contracts.
Approves correct invoices for payment.
Allocates transportation costs to relevant {{blank}} centers or orders.
This {{blank}} administrative effort and ensures billing accuracy.
Step five, performance monitoring and reporting.
TMS dashboards and {{blank}} tools measure KPIs such as on-time delivery rate (OTD), transportation cost per unit, carrier performance index, freight audit accuracy.
These insights help identify cost-saving opportunities and improve carrier relationships.
Four, technologies behind TMS.
Modern TMS platforms leverage advanced technologies to enhance {{blank}}.
AI and machine learning, predict delays, optimize carrier selection, forecast demand.
IoT, internet of things, real-{{blank}} vehicle and shipment tracking.
Cloud computing, scalability, global accessibility, and reduced IT overhead.
Blockchain, secure and transparent freight documentation and payment.
Big data analytics, freight spend analysis and route performance insights.
Five {{blank}} of a TMS.
Implementing a TMS brings several strategic and operational benefits.
Cost reduction, {{blank}} routes, carrier selection and load consolidation, lower freight costs.
Enhanced visibility, real-time tracking and predictive alerts, improve control.
Improved {{blank}}, automation reduces manual effort and errors.
Customer satisfaction, accurate ETAs and faster deliveries enhance service levels.
Data-driven decisions, analytics improve planning, budgeting, and strategic sourcing.
Six challenges in TMS implementation.
Despite its benefits, organizations must manage certain challenges.
High initial cost, enterprise-grade TMS solutions can {{blank}} substantial investment.
Integration complexity, requires seamless linking with ERP, WMS, and carrier systems.
Data quality issues, poor master data can lead to incorrect optimization.
Change {{blank}}, employees need training to adapt to new digital workflows.
Seven types of TMS deployment.
On-premise TMS, installed locally, high control but expensive, best for large enterprises.
{{blank}}-based TMS, SaaS model, scalable and easy to deploy, best for SMEs and global logistics networks.
Hybrid TMS, combination of both models, best for firms needing flexibility and control.
Conclusion. The transportation management system TMS has evolved from a simple tracking {{blank}} into a powerful strategic platform.
It helps businesses balance cost, service, and sustainability while offering deep visibility and control over logistics {{blank}}.
In a world where transportation costs can make or break profitability, adopting a robust TMS is not just an option, it's a strategic necessity.
With the rise of cloud computing, AI, and IoT, the next generation of TMS platforms will enable predictive, {{blank}}, and fully integrated logistics ecosystems.
That's it for today. If this video helped you understand how TMS works, don't forget to hit like, share it with your team, and subscribe for more supply chain insights.
And tell me in the comments, is your organization using a TMS? If yes, how has it changed your logistics performance?
See you in the next video.

slides.title: Language Awareness — Passive Voice for Processes
slides.content:
Notice how the article describes what a TMS does. Business and technical English relies heavily on the passive voice when the process matters more than who performs it.
• is/are + past participle → describes what happens to goods
• modal + be + past participle → describes capability (can be tracked, should be optimized)
• have/has + been + past participle → describes changes and results (costs have been reduced)
Look at the examples below and notice how the focus shifts from the actor to the action itself.

words.word: Shipments are monitored across every stage of the supply chain.
Routes can be optimized based on real-time traffic data.
Delivery times have been reduced significantly since adopting a TMS.

practiceItems.prompt: Which of these sentences uses Passive Voice for Processes correctly?
practiceItems.answer: The teacher asked the students to compare the two cases.
options: She explains the plan yesterday to the whole class.
They was discussing the results after the meeting ended.
The team was completing the project just before the deadline.
The teacher asked the students to compare the two cases.
practiceItems.contextLine: The teacher asked the students to compare the two cases.

practiceItems.prompt: whole / plan / class / clearly / to / explained / TMS / the / the
practiceItems.answer: TMS explained the plan clearly to the whole class
practiceItems.contextLine: TMS explained the plan clearly to the whole class.

practiceItems.contextLine: The team completed the project just before the deadline.

practiceItems.answer: process step by step to the audience
options: three main ideas from the study
process step by step to the audience
the students to compare the two cases
plan clearly to the whole class
practiceItems.contextLine: TMS described the process step by step to the audience.

practiceItems.answer: The report focused on three main ideas from the study
practiceItems.contextLine: The report focused on three main ideas from the study.

practiceItems.contextLine: They discussed the results after the meeting ended.
